About: the minimum-time descent between two fixed points

Source

Concept
Brachistochrone: frictionless beads released from rest between fixed endpoints (0,0) → (Δx, Δy), y measured downward, v = √(2gy).
Serves
Probe what decides the travel time of a bead sliding between two fixed posts, and how track shape, gravity, and endpoint placement enter the race.
Inquiry
Five committed predictions: what decides the travel time, whether the steepest start wins, the effect of raising g, the effect of moving a post, and whether your own trial curve can beat the best of the field.
Misconception
"The shortest track must be the fastest — or else the steepest possible start must be." The race itself puts both to the test: trials that stay steep longer (plunge deeper) than the cycloid pay more in extra distance than they earn in speed.

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealThe optimum curve stays off the canvas until after the student has committed to what decides the race and tested a steep trial.
Cognitive conflictThe chord length is printed beside the straight chute so its measured time can be weighed against its length.
Invariant made visibleThe speed–time band plots every bead's speed history on one axis, with the arrival-speed line drawn for comparison.
Operational numbersEvery timer is the sim's own integration clock; the geometry panel shows R and θF so shape can be tracked through any sweep.
Honest failureA trial curve that climbs above the release level stalls its bead in view; the readout says it never arrives.
Formal layer optionalThe time functional and the cycloid equations sit behind the ∑ Formal toggle.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two posts, one drop

Let’s set up the race. Three smooth tracks join the same two points: the amber straight chute (its chord length is marked), a blue circular arc, and your violet trial curve. Identical beads are released together from rest, with no friction.

2 · Which factor decides?

Before anything moves, have a think. Which factor do you think determines which track is fastest?

3 · Run the race

Now let’s race. Press ▶ Play to release all the beads together. Watch which bead leads in the first instants, and which one reaches the post first. The Travel times panel now lists each track’s time — compare it with the marked chord length.

So, after the race: which bead reached the post first?

4 · Steeper is better?

Here’s a tempting idea. You could drag the violet handles so the trial plunges almost vertically at first. Is the fastest path simply the one that drops as steeply as possible at the beginning? What do you think?

5 · The optimum joins in

Time to bring in a new racer. The cyan optimum curve is now on the track, and the speed–time band is open. Race it against a deliberately steeper trial, then look at where every curve ends up on the speed axis.

6 · Stronger gravity

Let’s change the rules a little. Suppose you raise g while both posts stay exactly where they are. What do you think happens?

7 · Moving the far post

Now let’s move the finish. Suppose you drag the lower post farther away sideways, keeping its height fixed. What do you expect to happen to the optimum track?

8 · Beat it if you can

Last challenge, and it’s over to you. Can you construct a smooth trial curve that beats the cycloid?

Time of descent as a functional of the track shape. The speed comes only from the drop y, so the integrand weighs extra length against early speed.
The stationary curve: a cycloid traced by a circle of radius R rolling under the release line. θ is the rolling parameter, not a polar angle.
Closed forms used here: θF and R follow from Δx and Δy alone; L is the chord. Both times scale as 1/√g, so g never changes the winner.
Energy conservation: every bead arrives at the same speed whatever the track — only the timing of the speed differs.

The Physics

The brachistochrone · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim releases identical beads from rest on frictionless tracks that join the same two posts, and times each one. Johann Bernoulli posed the question it asks, which track is fastest, as a challenge in 1696, and the answer helped start the calculus of variations.

What you'll learn

  • How a bead's speed depends on how far it has dropped.
  • How the shape of a track sets its travel time.
  • What shape the fastest track has, and how the two posts pick it out.
  • How the gravitational acceleration g enters the race.
The opening setup: two posts, Δx = 1.5 m apart and Δy = 1 m of drop, and three tracks between them.

What's on screen

  • Straight line (amber): the chord between the posts, with its length marked.
  • Circular arc (blue): leaves the release post vertically and arrives at the finish post.
  • Your trial (violet): a smooth curve through three ◆ handles that you can drag.
  • Cycloid (cyan): a fourth track for the same posts, shown once it is revealed.
  • Bead labels: each bead shows its elapsed time and speed. At the finish a ✓ appears, and the first bead to arrive is tagged 1st.
  • Speed–time graph (below the stage): every bead's speed against time, with the dashed arrival-speed line.
See itRelease the beads together at the opening posts. Watch for: a timer beside each bead, and a ✓ as each one reaches the finish.

03

Speed comes only from the drop

On a frictionless track, the track's push on the bead does no work, so only gravity changes the bead's energy. A bead released from rest that has dropped a distance y below the release level has ½mv² = mgy:

The mass cancels. Δy is the drop from release to finish.

Speed depends on the drop and nothing else: not on the mass, and not on the shape of the track. At the opening posts that is √(2 × 9.81 × 1.00) = 4.43 m/s at the finish, for every bead.

A track that dips below the finish level, like the blue arc here (by 0.08 m), lets its bead go faster than that on the way, then slow down on the climb.

See itRace all four tracks at the opening posts. Watch for: every bead's label reaching 4.43 m/s, and every curve on the graph ending on the dashed line.
04

Travel time weighs length against speed

A small step ds of the track takes ds/v. Adding up the steps gives the travel time, where y(x) is the track's depth below the release level and y′ = dy/dx:

Time of descent as an integral over the track.

A longer track adds steps. A bead that is already fast makes each step shorter in time. A steep start raises v early, which helps every later step, but it also lengthens the path. So the time depends on the whole shape of the track, not on its length alone.

Opening posts, g = 9.81 m/s²lengthtime
Straight line1.803 m0.814 s
Circular arc2.129 m0.710 s
Cycloid1.930 m0.693 s

The straight line is the shortest of these tracks and the slowest.

See itRace again and compare the arrival times with the track lengths. Watch for: the amber bead, on the shortest track, arriving last.
05

The fastest track is a cycloid

Between two fixed posts, for a frictionless bead released from rest in uniform gravity, no track is faster than a cycloid. It is the path of a point on the rim of a circle of radius R that rolls along under the release level:

θ is the angle the circle has rolled through, in radians.
  • The cycloid leaves the release post vertically, so the bead gains speed early, then flattens so the extra path does not run away.
  • Any trial that differs from it is slower. At the opening posts the arc comes within 3% of it, yet it still loses.
See itRace the cycloid against the straight line, the arc and the opening violet trial. Watch for: the cyan bead arriving first, tagged 1st, just ahead of the blue one.
06

The two posts pick which cycloid

Every cycloid has the same shape; they differ in size R. At the finish post, x = Δx and y = Δy. Dividing the two equations of the cycloid cancels R and leaves the roll angle θF to be found from Δx/Δy; R then follows:

θF has no closed form, so the sim solves for it numerically.

At the opening posts, Δx/Δy = 1.5 gives θF = 175.8° (3.069 rad) and R = 0.501 m. Once Δx/Δy exceeds π/2 ≈ 1.571, θF passes 180°: the cycloid runs below the finish level, then climbs back to the post.

At Δx = 3 m the lowest point is 2R = 1.24 m below the release level, 0.24 m below the finish.

See itMove the finish post out to Δx = 3 m. Watch for: the cyan track dipping below the finish before it climbs back, and the roll angle reading 232°.
07

Gravity rescales the times, not the shape

Tcyc for the cycloid; Tline for the straight line, where L is the chord length.

θF, R and L are set by Δx and Δy alone, so g appears only under the square root. Changing g leaves every track where it is and multiplies every time by the same factor, 1/√g. Quadrupling g halves every time, so the order of arrival cannot change.

Δx Δy g

These sliders move the sim too.

See itRun the race at g = 6 m/s², then at g = 24 m/s². Watch for: the cycloid time halving, 0.886 s then 0.443 s, while R and θF stay the same.
08

Where it matters

  • The calculus of variations. Bernoulli posed the problem in 1696 as a public challenge. Newton, Leibniz, l'Hôpital and his brother Jakob all solved it. The method, finding the curve that makes an integral stationary, was developed by Euler and Lagrange and underlies Lagrangian mechanics.
  • Light and least time. Bernoulli's own solution treated the bead as a light ray in a medium where light travels faster the deeper it goes, and applied Fermat's principle of least time.
  • Huygens' pendulum clock. The same cycloid, as a bowl, is also a tautochrone: a bead released anywhere on it takes the same time to reach the bottom. Huygens used cycloidal guides to make a pendulum swing in equal times.
Go deeper: Bernoulli's light-ray argument
  • Cut the track into thin layers. In each layer the speed is v = √(2gy), and Snell's law says sin α / v stays constant along a ray, where α is the angle between the track and the vertical.
  • So the fastest track obeys sin α / √y = constant. On a cycloid, sin α = sin(θ/2) and √y = √(2R) sin(θ/2), so the ratio is 1/√(2R) at every point.
09

Summary

In one line. Between two posts, a frictionless bead released from rest is fastest on a cycloid, because travel time weighs a track's length against the speed gained early, and the shortest track is not the fastest.

Key points

  • Speed is √(2gy), so every bead arrives at √(2gΔy), but at different times.
  • The fastest track is a cycloid. Δx : Δy sets its roll angle and radius, and past 180° it dips below the finish.
  • g multiplies every time by 1/√g and changes no shape.

Common mix-ups

  • "The shortest track is the fastest." The straight line is the shortest track here and the slowest.
  • "The steeper the start, the faster the race." A steep start gains speed early but adds path. The cycloid starts vertical and balances the two; a trial that plunges further is slower.
  • "Stronger gravity changes the best shape." The shape depends only on Δx : Δy. Gravity rescales the times.

Things to try on your own

  • Reshape the violet trial again and again and watch best trial so far in the Travel times panel. Compare it with the cycloid's time.
  • Race at Δx = 0.5 m, Δy = 2 m, then at Δx = 4 m, Δy = 0.5 m. Compare how far apart the three times are in each case.
  • Set g = 1.6 m/s², then 25 m/s². Multiply each cycloid time by √g and compare the two products.
